How the U.S. “saved” Japan — and themselves in the process

The Japanese yen recently fell to a 40-year low — nearly 164 to the dollar. And for the first time since 1998, the U.S. stepped in itself to support the yen’s exchange rate.

But why would America even save someone else’s currency?

Because Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. government debt, with roughly $1.14 trillion in U.S. Treasuries. And that’s a real trap.

Because of the crisis, Japan spent $73 billion in the spring to support the yen. But it still fell. The question became: where do you get even more dollars? — Exactly, by dumping those same Treasuries.

But if they start doing that, yields on U.S. debt will shoot up. In other words, Japan’s problems suddenly become America’s problems.

And that’s when the U.S. came up with a workaround: Japan was given the ability to borrow the dollars it needed against its U.S. Treasuries — instead of selling them on the market.

And the U.S. itself, to support the yen, sold its euro reserves instead of dollars. So they strengthened the yen without weakening the dollar.

Formally, the U.S. was saving Japan and its currency. In reality, it was saving its own debt market, and with it, the stability of the entire dollar system.

When you owe the world trillions, a crisis for your creditor automatically becomes a crisis for you. And saving them is the only way to save yourself.

I wish I’d discovered this years ago… 🌿📖

📌 Rebase Tokens: Why Your Balance Can Change Without a Trade

Main Points
⏺ Some tokens automatically adjust holder balances through a rebase mechanism
⏺ Your token count can increase or decrease without a normal buy or sell
⏺ This post explains why “more tokens” doesn’t always mean “more money”

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol periodically recalculates balances, increasing or decreasing token amounts.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — to target a price, manage supply, or create a special monetary design.
3️⃣ The Trap — if your balance grows but price falls harder, you didn’t actually profit.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — exchanges, wallets, and DeFi protocols may not handle rebasing balances cleanly.
5️⃣ Practical Check — track your share of total supply, liquidity, and rebase rules, not just token count.

Final Thoughts

Rebase tokens change both price and quantity. Beginners see “more coins,” but the market prices real value.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

🇸🇾🇹🇷 Syria and Turkey: The Next Front, With Carefully Managed Denials

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz addressed Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkish this week. He accused the Turkish president of dragging Turkey into “dangerous adventures in Syria” and warned that Israel would not allow anyone to threaten its security.

Katz told Erdogan to confine himself to the speeches he gives in Turkey’s parliament — speeches that are, in Katz’s words, “detached from reality” — rather than test Israel’s resolve. 

Turkey’s Defense Ministry replied with a denial and a promise.

No Turkish military delegation was at Abu al-Duhur air base before or during Israel’s strike, Ankara said. Turkey also said Israeli operations against neighboring countries must not be normalized. It pledged to keep helping Syria build its own military capacity and infrastructure under the “one army” principle. 

No Turkish presence at the base. Continued Turkish help to build the military that will use it.

Syria’s foreign minister, Asaad al-Shaibani, also denied that Ankara was building a base at Abu al-Duhur. He told Axios there was no plan for a permanent Turkish deployment or Turkish forces at the airfield. The base, he said, was largely empty and was being restored for the Syrian Air Force. Turkish officers had visited for training and broader military cooperation. 

Shaibani also confirmed that Israel and Syria had discussed Turkish military activity in Syria before the strike. Reuters reported that he and Mossad chief Roman Gofman spoke by phone on August 14, with Turkish deployments, arms transfers, drones, and military assistance to Syria among the issues discussed. 

Israel says it warned Damascus not to permit a Turkish deployment at the base. Damascus says no such deployment was planned. Both accounts agree that Turkey’s military role in Syria was important enough to discuss before Israel bombed the runway.

Shaibani said Israel had no legitimate justification for the attack. He added that U.S.-mediated talks on a security arrangement had made significant progress, but that Israel later walked back its commitments and the agreement was never implemented. 

The official denials were followed by a less restrained message from inside Syria’s ruling family.

Hussein al-Sharaa, father of President Ahmed al-Sharaa, wrote on Facebook that Damascus’s restraint reflected international considerations and reconstruction needs, not weakness. Syrians, he said, could raise large fighting forces within days. “We have occupied land called the Golan Heights,” he wrote. “We will take it back — sooner or later.” 

Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc in Lebanon, which Damascus has worked to weaken, also condemned the Israeli strike as a violation of Syrian sovereignty. The statement put Hezbollah on the same side as a Syrian government working to cut Hezbollah’s own supply lines. 

Israel says it is preventing a Turkish threat. Turkey says it is supporting a Syrian army. Damascus says there was no Turkish deployment to prevent.

The runway was still bombed.
